text:
In 1943, the statistician Abraham Wald took on a wartime question. Which parts of a bomber are the most vulnerable? The evidence was the damage on the planes that made it home. And the military's instinct was to protect the parts with the most holes.

Wald's memos work through an example. Four hundred planes fly a mission... and three hundred fifty-nine come back. The two engines are more than a quarter of the plane. But they carry fewer than one in five of the holes. The fuselage carries more than its share. So where are the missing engine hits? On the planes that never came back. In his numbers, one hit to an engine downs a plane thirty-nine times in a hundred. One to the fuselage... about five. The holes show where a plane can be hit and still come home. The protection belongs where they AREN'T.

Business data plays the same trick. Take five thousand simulated mutual funds, averaging six percent a year. Now close every fund that lost more than four percent, and drop it from the database. That's five hundred and fifteen funds... gone. Average the funds that are left, and you get seven point six five. Not one fund got better. The losers were just deleted.

The planes that made it home. The funds still open. The customers who stayed. When your data is whoever's still here... ask what's missing from it, and why. Even a fair sample, drawn from everyone, won't hit the truth exactly. So how far off can it be?
